motion.question: A trolley moves at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m s⁻² for 4.0 s. Connect the motion to its velocity–time graph, derive the constant-acceleration equations, and calculate displacement.

steps.title: Connect the trolley and graph
steps.prompt: Watch the trolley and graph share one clock. Predict the final velocity and explain why the trolley covers more distance during each successive second.
steps.answer: The velocity rises uniformly from 2.0 to 8.0 m s⁻¹, while the trolley moves increasingly quickly. At t = 4.0 s, its position is x = 20 m. The video runs slowly; the displayed t is the physical time.

steps.title: Derive velocity from gradient
steps.prompt: Read the highlighted rise and run. Starting with acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time, rearrange to express the final velocity.
steps.answer: The rise is v − u = 6.0 m s⁻¹ and the run is 4.0 s, so the constant gradient is a = 1.5 m s⁻². Rearranging a = (v − u)/t gives v − u = at and then v = u + at.

steps.title: Explain why area is displacement
steps.prompt: Match the narrow graph strip to the highlighted short section of the journey. What quantity does height × width represent, and what happens when all the strips are added?
steps.answer: Over a sufficiently short time Δt, displacement is approximately vΔt. Its units are (m s⁻¹) × s = m. Adding the small displacements gives the area under the velocity–time graph, which is signed displacement. The animated strips illustrate this idea; the exact area is calculated in the next step.
steps.tex: \Delta s\approx v\Delta t,\qquad s=\text{area under the velocity–time graph}

steps.title: Turn two areas into SUVAT
steps.prompt: Identify the cyan rectangle and amber triangle. Replace the triangle height v − u using the gradient result, then add the two contributions.
steps.answer: The rectangle contributes ut = 8 m. The triangle contributes ½(v − u)t = ½at² = 12 m. Together s = ut + ½at² = 20 m. These are contributions to the same journey, rather than two successive stages of motion.

steps.title: Compare gradient with area
steps.prompt: Find acceleration from the gradient and displacement from the trapezium area. Explain the different units and state when this SUVAT derivation is valid.
steps.answer: Gradient gives acceleration, 1.5 m s⁻². Area gives displacement, 20 m. The straight v–t line represents constant acceleration, which is required for these SUVAT equations. Velocity stays positive in this example, so distance equals displacement. A curved line has a changing gradient and needs another area method.

motion.pitfall: This fixed worked example uses u = 2.0 m s⁻¹, a = 1.5 m s⁻² and t = 4.0 s. The live model can use different parameter settings. Graph area gives signed displacement; it equals distance here because velocity stays positive. The strip argument uses a short-time approximation; the rectangle and triangle give the exact area for this straight-line graph. SUVAT requires constant acceleration. Measurement uncertainty is practised separately in the worksheet.

displacement.question: A robot travels east at 3.0 m s⁻¹ for 4.0 s and west at 2.0 m s⁻¹ for 3.0 s. Ignore the short turning interval. Take east as positive and compare displacement, distance, average velocity and average speed.

steps.title: Trace the eastward leg
steps.prompt: Watch the robot travel to the right. What position and signed graph area does it reach at 4.0 s?
steps.answer: The robot reaches x = +12 m. The area above the time axis is +12 m.

steps.title: Trace the westward leg
steps.prompt: Watch the robot reverse direction. Why is its second velocity–time area negative?
steps.answer: West is the negative direction. The second leg changes position by −6.0 m, leaving the robot at x = +6.0 m.

steps.title: Compare the two totals
steps.prompt: Compare the START and FINISH positions with the two shaded graph regions. Which areas cancel, and which must be added positively?
steps.answer: Displacement is +6.0 m east; total distance is 18 m. The returning leg partly cancels displacement but still adds to distance.

steps.title: Use the same total time
steps.prompt: Divide each total by 7.0 s. Why are average speed and the magnitude of average velocity different?
steps.answer: Average speed is 2.57 m s⁻¹ and average velocity is +0.857 m s⁻¹. They use different numerators. These displayed values retain extra digits for comparison.

displacement.pitfall: This question has two constant-velocity legs over 7.0 s. The live displacement simulation has one constant acceleration and a 6 s timeline, so it cannot reproduce this journey directly. Treat the turn as an idealised instantaneous velocity change; do not join the two velocity levels with a finite sloping interval or use a single SUVAT calculation for the whole journey.

vectors.question: Two horizontal forces act on a model boat: 6.0 N east and 8.0 N north. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant, then determine the third force needed for constant velocity.

steps.title: Build the component diagram
steps.prompt: Read the eastward and northward force arrows drawn from the same origin. Which components will the resultant have?
steps.answer: The joining diagonal is the resultant. Its perpendicular components are 6.0 N east and 8.0 N north.

steps.title: Find the diagonal length
steps.prompt: Why is the resultant magnitude less than 6.0 + 8.0 N? Use the right-angled triangle.
steps.answer: The forces act in perpendicular directions. Pythagoras gives a resultant of 10 N.

steps.title: Measure from east
steps.prompt: Watch the angle arc start at the positive horizontal axis. Which component is opposite this angle?
steps.answer: The northward component is opposite. The resultant points 53.1° north of east.

steps.title: Balance the resultant
steps.prompt: Watch the third force point opposite to the resultant. What happens to the net force and acceleration when it is added?
steps.answer: A 10 N force opposite the resultant makes the net force zero. The boat then has zero acceleration and can maintain its existing velocity.
steps.tex: \mathbf F_3=(-6.0\,\hat{\mathbf i}-8.0\,\hat{\mathbf j})\ \mathrm N,\qquad \sum\mathbf F=0\Rightarrow\mathbf a=0

vectors.pitfall: The live vector model can reproduce this example using Force A = 6 N, Angle A = 0°, Force B = 8 N, Angle B = 90°. Playback constructs a force diagram; it does not show the boat's trajectory. Zero net force means constant velocity, which may be nonzero. The direction must state its reference axis.

newton.question: A 4.0 kg trolley is pulled horizontally by 14 N. A constant resistance of 2.0 N opposes motion. Calculate its acceleration, connect an acceleration–pulling-force graph to mass, and identify the forces acting on the trolley.

steps.title: Read the opposing force arrows
steps.prompt: Take the pulling direction as positive. What remains when the resistance arrow is subtracted from the pulling-force arrow?
steps.answer: The resultant horizontal force is +12 N. Use the resultant, not the pulling force alone, in Newton's second law.

steps.title: Predict the change in velocity
steps.prompt: Divide the resultant by the trolley's mass. What does the answer say about the velocity change in each second?
steps.answer: The acceleration is +3.0 m s⁻², so velocity increases by 3.0 m s⁻¹ each second while these forces remain constant.

steps.title: Observe a force sweep
steps.prompt: Follow the line for fixed mass and resistance as pulling force increases. What are the gradient and vertical intercept of this acceleration–force graph?
steps.answer: The gradient is 1/m = 0.25 kg⁻¹ and the intercept is −Fresist/m = −0.50 m s⁻². The trolley must still move in the original direction for the assumed resistance direction to remain valid.

steps.title: Separate equilibrium from a third-law pair
steps.prompt: Compare the upward normal force and downward weight on the trolley. They balance vertically; why are they not a Newton’s third-law pair?
steps.answer: Both act on the trolley. Weight pairs with the trolley's gravitational force on Earth; the normal force pairs with the trolley's contact force on the track. Third-law partners act on different objects.
steps.tex: N-mg=0\quad\text{(vertical equilibrium)},\qquad\mathbf F_{A\to B}=-\mathbf F_{B\to A}\quad\text{(third law)}

newton.pitfall: The live lab above models vertical falling motion with speed-dependent drag. This worked example instead uses a horizontal trolley and constant resistance. The acceleration–pulling-force line assumes fixed mass and resistance while the trolley still moves forwards; the negative intercept represents deceleration, not a rule for friction after reversal. Force arrows are schematic. No initial velocity or trolley trajectory is assumed.
